sections.h2: How do I sell a house fast in New Brunswick, NJ?
sections.html:
Most New Brunswick owners choose between three routes: list with an agent, sell on their own, or take an as-is cash offer. Each route ends the same way, with a deed recorded at the Middlesex County Clerk's office on Bayard Street in the city itself. What changes is how long the house sits, who pays for repairs, and how much of the sale price reaches you.

New Brunswick is a renter city. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied rate for 2020 to 2024 at 21.4%, with 15,676 households averaging 3.13 people. A sale here often involves a house with tenants or a landlord seller, so the rental rules covered below matter as much as the repair list.

  • List with an agent: widest exposure, but showings, repairs and a closing timeline set by the buyer's lender.
  • Sell it yourself: saves a commission, yet you still need an attorney, a deed and the municipal paperwork described below.
  • Cash offer: usually no lender and a closing date you choose, with the house sold as it stands.

sections.h2: What is New Brunswick like for a home seller?
sections.html:
New Brunswick is a compact river city of 5.23 square miles of land on the Raritan, in Middlesex County, about halfway between New York City and Philadelphia. It borders Piscataway, Highland Park and Edison across the river, plus North Brunswick, East Brunswick and Franklin Township in Somerset County. The Census Bureau estimates 57,133 residents as of July 1, 2025.

The settlement dates to 1681 and took the New Brunswick name in 1714. It was incorporated as a town in 1736 and chartered as a city in 1784. Rutgers, founded in 1766 as Queen's College, has been in the city since 1771, and Old Queens, finished in 1811, is still its oldest building.

The city has been divided into wards for reference, and residents name areas such as the Fifth Ward, Feaster Park, Lincoln Park, Raritan Gardens and Edgebrook-Westons Mills. When you describe your house to a buyer, naming the section it sits in gives a clearer picture than the street address alone.

sections.h2: Who is buying homes in New Brunswick?
sections.html:
Demand here is driven by healthcare, the university and commuting. The city markets itself as the Health Care City and is home to the world headquarters of Johnson & Johnson, along with several medical teaching and research institutions. Rutgers has three campuses inside city limits, and Robert Wood Johnson Medical School sits in New Brunswick and Piscataway.

Commuting also shapes who looks at a house. The Census Bureau reports a mean travel time to work of 23.3 minutes for residents, and the city sits on the Northeast Corridor rail line between New York and Trenton.

  • Hospital and university staff looking for a short commute.
  • Landlords weighing a rental house against the city's rent control rules.
  • Households who want rail access to Penn Station on the Northeast Corridor.

sections.h2: What local steps apply before closing on a New Brunswick house?
sections.html:
Start with the fire safety inspection. The city's Division of Fire Safety performs smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm inspections on all one and two family homes for sale or lease, and there is an online application to schedule it. Book it early so a failed alarm does not delay the closing.

The Construction Department at 25 Kirkpatrick Street also handles a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy, which the city says to use when necessary. Call 732-745-5075, the department number on the city's permits page, and ask whether your sale needs one, because the answer depends on the property type and its history.

If the house has tenants, read the rent control rules before you list. Most rental units in New Brunswick fall under the city's Rent Control Ordinance, and regulated units must register every year by April 1. Owners of unregistered units face summonses and fines, so confirm your registration status with the Rent Control office before you list.

sections.h2: How does rent control affect selling a New Brunswick rental property?
sections.html:
It affects the income a buyer can count on. Rent increases are capped at the annual allowance set by the ordinance unless the unit has an approved vacancy decontrol or is exempt, so the rent roll you show is the ceiling a buyer will underwrite.

The city lists a registration fee of $55 per unit for 2027, with the same amount added again if filed after April 30. Vacancy adjustments cost $60 per unit and market vacancy decontrol $175. The Rent Control office takes questions at 732-745-5050 or rentcontrol@cityofnewbrunswick.org, and owners can also read about the November 2025 changes that took effect January 1, 2026.

sections.h2: What does the state charge a seller in New Brunswick?
sections.html:
The seller pays the state Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. For a sale of $350,000 or less it runs from $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000 up to $3.90 per $500 between $200,000 and $350,000, and the rates are higher above that figure.

If you live out of state, expect a separate filing. A nonresident seller must pay at least 2% of the deed consideration toward New Jersey gross income tax at closing on form GIT/REP-1, unless a seller assurance on form GIT/REP-3 applies. A New Jersey resident signs the GIT/REP-3 instead, and the settlement agent normally prepares both.

The Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied homes here at $353,800, which sits just above the $350,000 line. Above that line the state uses a second schedule that starts at $2.90 per $500 on the first $150,000 and reaches $4.80 per $500 between $200,000 and $550,000. Your closing attorney will show the exact fee on the settlement statement.

sections.h2: Where is the deed recorded and what must it contain?
sections.html:
Deeds for New Brunswick houses are recorded with the Middlesex County Clerk at 75 Bayard Street, fourth floor, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 4:10 pm, and you must arrive by 4 pm. The registry line is 732-745-3002. Appointments are not required, though people with appointments are served first.

  • The deed must be in English, legible and properly acknowledged, with original signatures and names printed beneath.
  • It must say "Prepared by" followed by the drafter's name, and list tax block, lot and consideration.
  • A record and return address is required on every recorded document.
  • Paper filings need a cover sheet; without one the county adds a $20 indexing charge.

Title companies and attorneys can also file through the county's e-recording portal, which accepts documents around the clock. The clerk also offers a free Property Alert Service by email, which notifies you when a document is recorded against your block and lot, a useful safeguard against deed fraud on a vacant property.

faqs.q: Can I sell my New Brunswick house with tenants still living in it?
faqs.a: Yes. A sale does not end a tenancy. Keep your rent control registration current and have the lease and rent history ready, since regulated units must register every year by April 1 and unregistered units can draw fines.

faqs.q: Do I need an inspection to sell a one or two family home in New Brunswick?
faqs.a: Yes, at least a smoke detector and carbon monoxide alarm inspection. The city's Division of Fire Safety performs it for one and two family homes for sale or lease. Ask the Construction Department at 732-745-5075 whether a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy is also needed.

faqs.q: Who records the deed after a sale in New Brunswick?
faqs.a: The Middlesex County Clerk's registry, in the County Administration Building on Bayard Street in New Brunswick. Your closing attorney or title company normally submits it, on paper or electronically.

faqs.q: What if I own the house but live outside New Jersey?
faqs.a: You will complete a GIT/REP form at closing. A nonresident seller prepays at least 2% of the deed consideration toward gross income tax unless an exemption on the GIT/REP-3 applies, and may claim a refund later if the tax owed is lower.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer fee on a $350,000 sale?
faqs.a: On a sale of exactly $350,000 the state schedule charges $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 per $500 from $150,000 to $200,000, and $3.90 per $500 from $200,000 to $350,000. A price even slightly above $350,000 moves the whole sale to a higher schedule.
